blocks.text: Priesthood was an institution of mediation: Israel’s priests served in sacrifice, taught holiness, blessed the people, guarded sacred space, and represented access to God. In the Second Temple world, temple service remained central, and legitimate priestly descent was a live concern. Hebrews 7 sets its argument within that framework but links the arrival of a different priesthood with a change in law and with the introduction of a better hope through which people approach God.

Israel’s priesthood is rooted in the wilderness sanctuary and tabernacle, continues in temple worship, and reappears in the Second Temple world. That long institutional background clarifies why Hebrews repeatedly discusses descent, appointment, sacrifice, and continuity when comparing the Levitical priests with Jesus.

Hebrews reads the presentation of Melchizedek in Genesis 14 together with Psalm 110 and treats him as a literary analogy for Jesus’ enduring priesthood. The description “without father, without mother, without genealogy” need not mean that Melchizedek literally had no parents, and Hebrews does not identify the Genesis figure as Jesus. The comparison rests on how Melchizedek appears in the scriptural account and how that portrayal serves the chapter’s argument.

The chapter’s statements about changing the priesthood, setting aside a former commandment, and establishing a better covenant belong to its differentiated argument about law and priesthood. They do not authorize lawlessness or the conclusion that Torah has no continuing Jewish meaning. Reading the covenant contrast as contempt for Judaism or as erasure of living Jewish communities is therefore not a safe interpretive shortcut.

For the transmission of Hebrews as a whole, Papyrus 46 is an early and substantial witness, although it contains gaps and its estimated date remains approximate. Codex Sinaiticus also preserves Hebrews, placing it in its New Testament sequence after 2 Thessalonians.

Christian interpretation has often read Leviticus through the priestly and covenant arguments developed in Hebrews 7–10. That is a later canonical reception of Leviticus and should be distinguished from Leviticus’s own instructions to Israel.

sections.title: The Wider Text and Its Reception
